content: Brugia malayi is a parasitic filarial roundworm responsible for causing filariasis in humans. It was first identified by Lichtenstein and later named Filaria malayi by Brug in 1927, distinguishing it from Wuchereria bancrofti. In 1958, Buckley proposed a separate genus, Brugia, and the organism was renamed Brugia malayi. This parasite is geographically restricted to tropical regions of Asia. The life cycle of Brugia malayi begins when infective larvae are transmitted to a human host through the bite of an infected arthropod during a blood meal. Once inside the host, the larvae migrate to specific sites in the body, where they mature into adult worms capable of producing microfilariae. These adult worms reside in human tissues, particularly in the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, where they can survive for several years. Similar to Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi primarily inhabits the lymphatic system. Female worms produce microfilariae, which circulate in the bloodstream and are subsequently ingested by mosquitoes during a blood meal. Within the mosquito, the microfilariae develop over 1 to 2 weeks into infective third-stage larvae (filariform larvae). During a subsequent blood meal, these larvae are transmitted to a new vertebrate host, where they migrate to the lymphatic system and mature into adult worms over a period of up to 18 months. Recent research has revealed that Brugia malayi harbors an endosymbiotic bacterium, Wolbachia, throughout all stages of its life cycle. The genome of Wolbachia was sequenced at New England Biolabs. Experimental studies have shown that treatment of the human host with doxycycline can eliminate Wolbachia. Nematodes that are cured of Wolbachia become sterile and exhibit increased morbidity. The laboratory diagnosis of Brugia malayi infection primarily involves the microscopic identification of microfilariae in blood samples. Blood collection should be timed to coincide with the known periodicity of microfilariae in the bloodstream. Thick blood smears stained with Giemsa or hematoxylin and eosin are commonly used for this purpose. To enhance sensitivity, concentration techniques such as centrifugation of blood lysed in 2% formalin (Knott's technique) or filtration through a Nucleopore membrane can be employed. Antigen detection using immunoassays for circulating filarial antigens is a valuable diagnostic method, particularly in cases where microfilaremia is low or variable. Molecular diagnostic techniques, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), are also available. Identification of adult worms can be achieved through tissue samples obtained during nodulectomies (as in onchocerciasis), subcutaneous biopsies, or removal of worms from the eye (as in loiasis). On September 20, 2007, scientists successfully mapped the genome of Brugia malayi, the parasitic worm responsible for lymphatic filariasis, also known as elephantiasis. Understanding the genetic content of this organism may pave the way for the development of novel drugs and vaccines to combat the disease.
